title: Prophet Adam (آدم) - The First Human & Prophet
display_title: Prophet Adam The First Human & Prophet
narrative:
• Creation: Allah gathered clays of various colors and textures from all over the Earth to create Adam (hence humanity's varied skins and temperaments, as noted in Hadith). Allah shaped him from sound-emitting clay (Salsal) and breathed His created soul into him. When the soul reached his eyes, Adam looked at the fruits of Paradise; when it reached his nose, he sneezed and said, "Alhamdulillah" (Praise be to Allah).
• The Angels and Iblis: Allah taught Adam the names and properties of all creations - a knowledge angels did not possess. Demonstrating Adam's superior capacity to learn, Allah commanded the angels to bow to Adam in respect. All prostrated except Iblis (Satan), who was a Jinn elevated among angels. Iblis arrogantly refused, saying: "I am better than him: You created me from fire and created him from clay" (7:12). Allah expelled Iblis, who requested respite until Judgment Day to mislead humanity.
• The Forbidden Tree & The Loss of Garments: Allah placed Adam and Hawwa (Eve) in Paradise, allowing them to eat from anywhere except one specific tree. Iblis whispered to them, swearing by Allah that he was a sincere advisor, falsely claiming: "Your Lord only forbade you this tree lest you become angels or become immortal" (7:20).
• Exposing the Awrah: As soon as Adam and Hawwa tasted from the tree, the divine garments covering them vanished instantly, exposing their private parts (Awrah). Feeling deeply ashamed, they frantically began picking leaves from the trees of Paradise and sewing them together to cover their bodies (7:22, 20:121).
• Repentance and Descent: Allah called out to them regarding their disobedience. Instead of making excuses like Iblis, Adam and Hawwa repented using words Allah inspired them with: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers" (7:23). Allah accepted their repentance, but decreed that Adam, Hawwa, and Iblis descend to Earth to live, struggle, and die.

title: Prophet Idris (إدريس) / Enoch
narrative:
• Idris lived during the generations between Adam and Nuh. Classical scholars of Tafsir (like Ibn Kathir) note he was the first human to write with a reed pen, sew and wear tailored cloth garments (instead of animal skins), and study weapon design and astronomy.
• Allah praised him in the Quran: "And mention in the Book, Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet. And We raised him to a high station" (19:56-57).
• During the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj), Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) met Idris residing in the fourth heaven.

title: Prophet Nuh (نوح) / Noah
narrative:
• Origin of Idolatry: For ten generations after Adam, humanity lived on Monotheism. Eventually, five pious men died (Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr). Satan convinced the people to erect statues of these men in their gathering places to remember their piety. After those generations passed, knowledge was lost, and people began worshiping the statues directly.
• Preaching for 950 Years: Allah sent Nuh to call them back to God. He preached tirelessly day and night, publicly and in secret, for 950 years (29:14). His people placed their fingers in their ears, wrapped themselves in their garments, and mocked him continuously.
• Building the Ark: When Allah informed Nuh that no more of his people would believe, Nuh prayed for judgment. Allah commanded him to build a giant three-story Ark (Fulk) on dry land. His people walked past him and ridiculed him for building a ship away from any water.
• The Deluge and the Lost Son: The sign for the punishment was water gushing forth from a domestic clay oven (Tannur). Heavy rain poured from the skies while springs erupted from the ground. Nuh brought onto the Ark a male and female of every creature, along with the small group of believers. Nuh saw his non-believing son (Kanaan/Yam) standing isolated and called out: "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers!" His son replied: "I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me from the water." Nuh warned him that nothing could save him that day, and a massive wave surged between them, drowning his son (11:42-43).
• The Aftermath: The Ark rested on Mount Judi (in modern Turkey/border region). Nuh released the animals, and humanity restarted through his three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

title: Prophet Hud (هود) & The People of 'Ad
narrative:
• The Greatness of 'Ad: The people of 'Ad lived in Al-Ahqaf (sand dunes between Oman and Yemen). They were giants of physical stature and built towering monuments (Iram of the Pillars). They believed no power on Earth could match them, boasting: "Who is greater than us in strength?" (41:15). They fell into idol worship and tyranny.
• Hud's Call: Prophet Hud reminded them that their strength was a blessing from Allah and warned them against oppression. They accused him of madness and foolishness.
• The Destruction: Allah sent a long drought. Seeing a dense black cloud approaching over their valleys, the people of 'Ad celebrated, assuming it was rain. Hud warned them it was the promised punishment. A roaring, freezing windstorm (Sarsar) engulfed them, raging continuously for seven nights and eight days. It ripped people off their feet and slammed them down, leaving their hollow, decapitated bodies scattered like uprooted palm trunks (69:6-8). Hud and the believers were saved.

title: Prophet Salih (صالح) & The People of Thamud
display_title: Prophet Salih & The People of Thamud
narrative:
• The Rock Carvers: The people of Thamud succeeded 'Ad, inhabiting Al-Hijr (Mada'in Salih in Saudi Arabia). They carved luxury homes directly out of solid mountain rock faces.
• The Miracle She-Camel: Demanding a miraculous sign, they challenged Salih to produce a giant, pregnant she-camel from a specific giant boulder. Salih prayed, and by Allah's power, the boulder split open, and a she-camel stepped out. Salih established a divine rule: the she-camel would drink from the town's water well on one full day (supplying the town with endless fresh milk in return), and the town would use the water on the alternate day.
• The Crime: Driven by arrogance and a desire to drink water without sharing, nine wicked leaders led by Qudar ibn Salif plotted to kill the camel. They ambushed her, hamstrung her legs with a sword, and slaughtered her.
• The Destruction: Salih warned them: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied" (11:65). On the first day their faces turned yellow, on the second day red, and on the third day black. On the fourth morning, a deafening sonic blast (Sayhah) coupled with a massive earthquake struck them, leaving them lifeless in their homes.

title: Prophet Ibrahim (إبراهيم) / Abraham - Friend of Allah (Khalilullah)
display_title: Prophet Ibrahim Abraham Friend of Allah
narrative:
• Search for Truth & Confronting Azar: Ibrahim grew up in Babylon. His father Azar was a chief craftsman of idols. Ibrahim observed the stars, the moon, and the sun, pointing out to his people that because these celestial bodies set and fade, they cannot be divine; only the Creator of the heavens and earth deserves worship (6:75-79).
• Smashing the Idols: During an annual festival when the townsfolk left, Ibrahim entered the temple and smashed all idols with an axe, leaving only the largest idol intact and resting the axe on its shoulder. When questioned, Ibrahim said: "Ask the big one, if they can speak!" They admitted idols cannot speak, yet they refused to leave their paganism out of pride.
• The Miraculous Fire: King Namrud (Nimrod) ordered Ibrahim to be burned alive. They constructed a massive bonfire and launched Ibrahim into it via a catapult. Allah commanded the fire: "O fire, be cool and peaceful for Ibrahim" (21:69). The ropes burned off, but Ibrahim walked out of the roaring flames completely unharmed.
• The Settlement at Makkah: Ibrahim migrated to the Levant with his wife Sarah. Later, Sarah gifted her maidservant Hajar to Ibrahim, who bore him his firstborn son, Ismail. Under divine command, Ibrahim took Hajar and infant Ismail to the uncultivated, waterless valley of Makkah. When Hajar realized this was Allah's command, she said: "Then He will not abandon us." Running seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah seeking water, Angel Jibreel struck the earth, causing the Zamzam spring to gush forth.
• The Ultimate Sacrifice: When Ismail reached youth, Ibrahim saw a recurring dream where he was sacrificing his son. Upon telling Ismail, the boy replied: "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient" (37:102). Satan tried three times to tempt Ibrahim and Ismail to disobey on their way to Mina (which became the ritual of Rami al-Jamarat - stoning Satan). As Ibrahim placed the knife on Ismail's neck, Allah called out that the test was fulfilled, replacing Ismail with a ram from Paradise.
• Building the Kaaba: Ibrahim and Ismail built the foundations of the Kaaba, praying for a Prophet to be sent from their offspring - a prayer answered thousands of years later through Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

title: Prophet Lut (لوط) / Lot
narrative:
• The Sins of Sodom: Lut, the nephew of Ibrahim, was sent to the towns of Sodom and Gomorrah near the Dead Sea. The inhabitants committed unprecedented open sins: public homosexuality, ambush of travelers, robbery, and refusing to harbor guests properly.
• The Heavenly Guests: Angels disguised as handsome young men visited Lut's home. Lut felt distressed, knowing his town's evil habits. His wife, who secretly supported the town's wicked practices, snuck out and informed the townsfolk that handsome men were in Lut's house. An aggressive mob surrounded Lut's home, demanding access to his guests. Lut pleaded with them, offering his daughters (meaning the respectable women of the town through lawful marriage), but they sneered and refused.
• The Punishment: The angels revealed their identity to Lut, saying: "They will never reach you." Angel Jibreel struck the mob with his wing, blinding them. The angels instructed Lut to leave with his family during the last hours of the night and warned: "Let none of you look back - except your wife." At dawn, Jibreel inserted his wing beneath the cities, lifted them high into the sky until angels could hear the barking of the town's dogs, flipped the cities upside down, and rained down hard clay stones (Sijjil) marked specifically for each sinner. Lut's wife turned back to watch and was struck dead by a stone.

title: Prophet Ismail (إسماعيل) / Ishmael
narrative:
• Ismail was the eldest son of Ibrahim. His early life established core rituals of the Hajj pilgrimage: running between Safa and Marwah with his mother Hajar, the emergence of Zamzam, and his willingness to be sacrificed for Allah's command.
• He learned Arabic from the nomadic Jurhum tribe that settled near Makkah around the Zamzam well and married into them.
• Together with his father Ibrahim, he raised the walls of the Kaaba. The Quran highlights his character: "And mention in the Book, Ismail. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet. He used to enjoin on his family prayer and zakah and was to his Lord pleasing" (19:54-55).
• From his lineage descended the Adnanite Arabs and ultimately Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).

title: Prophet Ishaq (إسحاق) / Isaac
narrative:
• Ishaq was Ibrahim's second son, born to his first wife, Sarah.
• Angels visited Ibrahim on their way to destroy the people of Lut. They gave Sarah news of a son named Ishaq, and after him, a grandson named Ya'qub. Sarah, being an elderly infertile woman, struck her forehead in amazement and laughed, saying: "Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman and my husband here is an old man?" The angels responded: "Do you wonder at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house" (11:72-73).
• Ishaq was a righteous prophet who continued his father's legacy in the Levant, becoming the forefather of the Israelite line of prophets.

title: Prophet Ya'qub (يعقوب) / Jacob (Israel)
narrative:
• Son of Ishaq, also designated in the Quran by the title Israel (meaning "Servant of God"). He had 12 sons, who formed the 12 Tribes of Israel.
• Ya'qub loved his son Yusuf deeply, recognizing his spiritual promise. When Yusuf's envious older brothers claimed a wolf had eaten Yusuf and presented his shirt stained with fake sheep's blood, Ya'qub saw through their deceit. Instead of succumbing to rage, he declared: "Beautiful patience (Sabrun Jameel), and Allah is the one sought for help against what you describe" (12:18).
• Ya'qub wept out of grief for decades until his pupils turned white and he lost his sight. Yet he told his sons: "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah... do not despair of relief from Allah" (12:86).
• When Yusuf revealed his identity from Egypt decades later and sent his shirt back, Ya'qub wiped it over his face and his eyesight was restored. He brought his entire family to Egypt, fulfilling Yusuf's vision.

title: Prophet Yusuf (يوسف) / Joseph
surah_citations: Surah Yusuf (12:1-111) (Narrated sequentially as "The Best of Stories").
narrative:
• The Dream and the Well: Young Yusuf dreamed that eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrated to him. Ya'qub advised him not to tell his brothers. Driven by jealousy, his ten older brothers threw Yusuf into a dark, dry well, stole his shirt, stained it with fake blood, and lied to their father. A passing caravan retrieved Yusuf from the well and sold him as a slave in Egypt to the Aziz (governor/chief minister).
• The Temptation of Zulaikha: As Yusuf grew into a remarkably handsome man, the Aziz's wife (Zulaikha) locked the palace doors and tried to seduce him. Yusuf sought refuge in Allah and ran for the door. She chased him, grabbing and tearing his shirt from the back. The Aziz appeared at the door. Zulaikha falsely accused Yusuf, but a wise relative noted: "If his shirt is torn from the front, she spoke truth; but if torn from the back, she lied." His shirt was torn from behind, proving Yusuf's innocence.
• The Banquet and Prison: To justify her actions to local women who gossiped about her, Zulaikha held a banquet, handing each woman a sharp knife and fruit. When Yusuf stepped into the room, the women were so dazzled by his supernatural beauty that they sliced their own hands without realizing it, crying: "Perfect is Allah! This is no human; this is a noble angel!" (12:31). Preferring righteousness to sin, Yusuf prayed to be sent to prison rather than succumb to corruption.
• Prison and Dream Interpretation: In prison, Yusuf preached monotheism and interpreted the dreams of two fellow inmates (the royal baker and cupbearer). Years later, the King of Egypt had a troubled dream: seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean cows, and seven green ears of grain next to seven dry ones. The cupbearer remembered Yusuf, who interpreted the dream accurately: seven years of abundant harvests followed by seven years of severe famine.
• Exoneration and Authority: Yusuf requested his name be cleared before leaving prison. The women and Zulaikha confessed their deceit. The King appointed Yusuf as Grand Treasurer (Aziz) over Egypt. When the famine struck, Yusuf's brothers traveled to Egypt for food supplies. Yusuf recognized them, tested their honesty regarding their youngest brother Binyamin, and eventually revealed his identity: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother." He forgave them completely: "No blame upon you today; Allah will forgive you" (12:92).

A passing caravan retrieved Yusuf from the well and sold him as a slave in Egypt to the Aziz (governor/chief minister).

narrative_points.label: The Temptation of Zulaikha
narrative_points.detail: As Yusuf grew into a remarkably handsome man, the Aziz's wife (Zulaikha) locked the palace doors and tried to seduce him. Yusuf sought refuge in Allah and ran for the door. She chased him, grabbing and tearing his shirt from the back. The Aziz appeared at the door. Zulaikha falsely accused Yusuf, but a wise relative noted: "If his shirt is torn from the front, she spoke truth; but if torn from the back, she lied." His shirt was torn from behind, proving Yusuf's innocence.

narrative_points.label: The Banquet and Prison
narrative_points.detail: To justify her actions to local women who gossiped about her, Zulaikha held a banquet, handing each woman a sharp knife and fruit. When Yusuf stepped into the room, the women were so dazzled by his supernatural beauty that they sliced their own hands without realizing it, crying: "Perfect is Allah! This is no human; this is a noble angel!" (12:31). Preferring righteousness to sin, Yusuf prayed to be sent to prison rather than succumb to corruption.

narrative_points.label: Prison and Dream Interpretation
narrative_points.detail: In prison, Yusuf preached monotheism and interpreted the dreams of two fellow inmates (the royal baker and cupbearer). Years later, the King of Egypt had a troubled dream: seven fat cows being eaten by seven lean cows, and seven green ears of grain next to seven dry ones. The cupbearer remembered Yusuf, who interpreted the dream accurately: seven years of abundant harvests followed by seven years of severe famine.

narrative_points.label: Exoneration and Authority
narrative_points.detail: Yusuf requested his name be cleared before leaving prison. The women and Zulaikha confessed their deceit. The King appointed Yusuf as Grand Treasurer (Aziz) over Egypt. When the famine struck, Yusuf's brothers traveled to Egypt for food supplies. Yusuf recognized them, tested their honesty regarding their youngest brother Binyamin, and eventually revealed his identity: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother." He forgave them completely: "No blame upon you today; Allah will forgive you" (12:92).

lessons: Remaining chaste under pressure; forgiving those who mistreated you when you hold power over them; divine planning turns trials into triumphs.

title: Prophet Shu'ayb (شعيب) & The People of Madyan
display_title: Prophet Shu'ayb & The People of Madyan
narrative:
• Economic Corruption: Shu'ayb was sent to Madyan and the dwellers of the wood (Ashab al-Aykah near the Red Sea). Besides worshiping a sacred tree, they were dishonest traders who cheated customers by giving short measure and weight (Al-Mikyal wal-Mizan) while highway-robbing passing merchants.
• The Eloquent Orator: Known in Islamic literature as Khatib al-Anbiya (The Speaker of the Prophets) for his clear speech, Shu'ayb reasoned with them: "Give full measure and weight and do not deprive people of their due rights, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation" (7:85). They mocked him: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshiped or that we stop doing with our wealth what we please?" (11:87).
• The Destruction: They threatened to stone Shu'ayb and banish the believers. Allah sent an unbearable, suffocating heat wave for seven days. Then a cloud appeared overhead, offering shade. The people gathered underneath it for relief, whereupon the cloud rained fire down upon them, accompanied by a roaring blast (Sayhah) and a violent earthquake that left them lifeless in their homes.

title: Prophet Ayyub (أيوب) / Job
narrative:
• The Great Trial: Ayyub was a wealthy prophet blessed with large herds of livestock, fertile lands, many children, and excellent health. Allah tested him by removing his wealth, his land, his children, and his health. He suffered from a severe skin illness for 18 years (as recorded in Hadith), leaving him isolated outside his town. Only his devoted wife stayed by his side, working manual labor to buy food.
• Supplication and Healing: Through 18 years of extreme physical pain, Ayyub never complained against Allah. When people began saying his illness was due to a hidden sin, Ayyub raised his hands in gentle prayer: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful" (21:83).
• Restoration: Allah commanded Ayyub: "Strike the ground with your foot; this is a cool spring for washing and drinking" (38:42). Ayyub bathed in and drank from the spring, and his body was restored to perfect health. Allah returned his family, doubled his wealth (authentic Hadith state Allah rained golden locusts down upon him), and blessed his life.

title: Prophet Dhul-Kifl (ذو الكفل) / Ezekiel or Isaiah
display_title: Prophet Dhul Kifl Ezekiel or Isaiah
narrative:
• The name Dhul-Kifl means "The One of the Pledge" or "He who fulfilled his covenant." Classical commentators note he was a prophet who took up a leadership pledge after Prophet Al-Yasa'.

Satan attempted multiple times to incite Dhul-Kifl to anger through irritating court disputes, but Dhul-Kifl maintained complete composure and fulfilled his pledge flawlessly.

title: Prophet Musa (موسى) & Prophet Harun (هارون)
surah_citations: Appears in over 30 Surahs including Al-Baqarah, Al-A'raf, Taha, Ash-Shu'ara, Al-Qasas, Al-Ahqaf, An-Naziat.
narrative:
• Infancy & The Palace: Pharaoh (Fir'awn) was warned by astrologers that an Israelite boy would bring down his empire. He ordered all newborn Israelite boys killed every alternate year. Musa was born in a year of slaughter. Allah inspired his mother to put baby Musa in a wooden chest and float him down the River Nile. Pharaoh's wife, Asiya, found the chest, fell in love with the baby, and convinced Pharaoh to adopt him: "He may be of benefit to us, or we may adopt him as a son" (28:9). Allah caused Musa to refuse all Egyptian wet nurses, leading him back to his biological mother to be nursed.
• Flight to Madyan: As a young man, Musa saw an Egyptian guard beating an Israelite. Musa struck the Egyptian with his fist to break up the fight, accidentally killing him. Fleeing Egypt in fear, Musa walked through the desert to Madyan. At a water well, he helped two young women water their flock while men shoved past them. Musa sat under the shade and prayed: "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need" (28:24). Their father (a pious elder) hired Musa to work for 8 to 10 years, and Musa married one of the daughters (Saffurah).
• The Burning Bush & Calling Pharaoh: Returning to Egypt at Mount Tur, Musa saw a fire on the mountain. When he approached, Allah spoke directly to him: "Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance" (20:14). Allah granted Musa two primary miracles: his wooden staff turned into a real serpent, and his hand shone with pure white light when tucked under his arm. Musa requested his brother Harun, an eloquent speaker, to join him. Together they confronted Pharaoh, asking him to free the enslaved Israelites.
• Duel with the Magicians: Pharaoh gathered Egypt's top sorcerers for a public contest on a festival day. The magicians threw down their ropes and rods, using optical magic to make them appear like slithering snakes. Musa threw down his staff, which transformed into a real python that swallowed all their illusions. Recognizing that this was divine power rather than magic, the sorcerers fell into prostration, declaring: "We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses." Pharaoh threatened to cut off their hands and feet on alternate sides and crucify them on palm trunks, but the magicians stood firm in their new faith.
• The Nine Signs and The Red Sea: Pharaoh hardened his heart. Allah sent Nine Signs upon Egypt: severe droughts, crop failures, floods, swarms of locusts, lice, frogs, and water turning into blood. Each time, Pharaoh promised to free the Israelites if the plague was removed, only to break his promise once it lifted. Finally, Musa led Banu Isra'il out of Egypt by night. Pharaoh pursued them with a massive army, trapping the Israelites at the Red Sea. The Israelites panicked, saying: "We are surely overtaken!" Musa declared: "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me" (26:61-62). Musa struck the sea with his staff; it parted into twelve dry paths with giant walls of water on either side. Musa and his people crossed safely. Pharaoh and his army rushed in after them, whereupon Allah collapsed the waters. As Pharaoh was drowning, he tried to repent: "I believe that there is no deity except Him in whom the Children of Israel believe." Angel Jibreel later mentioned (in authentic Hadith in Tirmidhi) that he stuffed dark mud into Pharaoh's mouth so he could not utter words that might attract Allah's mercy at the last second. Allah preserved Pharaoh's physical corpse as a sign for future generations (10:92).
• Desert Wandering & Golden Calf: While Musa spent 40 nights on Mount Sinai receiving the Torah tables, a man named Samiri fashioned a Golden Calf out of borrowed jewelry and used trickery to make it emit a lowing sound. The Israelites began worshiping it. Harun tried to stop them, but they nearly killed him. Musa returned, destroyed the calf, burned it, and scattered its ash in the sea. Banu Isra'il refused to fight the giants of Palestine, telling Musa: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight! We are sitting right here" (5:24). Allah cursed them to wander lost in the Sinai desert (Tih) for 40 years.

title: Prophet Dawud (داوود) / David
narrative:
• Defeating Goliath: Dawud began as a young, inexperienced shepherd boy in the army of King Talut (Saul). The enemy army was led by a giant warrior named Jalut (Goliath). While grown men feared Jalut, young Dawud stepped forward with a sling and stones. Reciting God's name, Dawud struck Jalut in the forehead, killing him instantly and causing the enemy army to flee.
• Kingship and Miracle of Iron: Allah granted Dawud both prophethood and kingship over Israel. Allah bestowed upon him the scripture called the Zabur (Psalms). Allah made iron soft in Dawud's hands like warm wax, without needing fire or hammers, allowing him to weave protective chainmail armor (Sard) for his soldiers.
• Beautiful Voice: Dawud possessed an exceptionally beautiful voice. When he recited the Zabur in praise of Allah, wild birds halted in mid-air and surrounding mountains joined in echoing his praises.
• Fast of Dawud: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) highlighted Dawud's personal worship in Sahih Hadith: he would sleep half the night, pray one-third, sleep one-sixth, and fast on alternate days (the most beloved fasting to Allah).

title: Prophet Sulaiman (سليمان) / Solomon
narrative:
• The Unmatched Kingdom: Son of Dawud, Sulaiman prayed to Allah: "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me" (38:35). Allah granted him control over the wind (moving his armies vast distances in hours), authority over Jinn (who built palaces, statues, and deep pools for him), and the ability to speak to animals, birds, and insects.
• The Valley of Ants: While marching with his massive army of Jinn, men, and birds, Sulaiman overheard an ant warning its community: "O ants, enter your dwellings lest Sulaiman and his soldiers crush you while they perceive not" (27:18). Sulaiman smiled and laughed at its words, praying to Allah in gratitude for his blessings.
• Queen of Sheba (Bilqis): A Hoopoe bird (Hudhud) brought news of a rich kingdom in Saba (Yemen) ruled by a queen whose people worshiped the sun. Sulaiman sent a letter beginning with Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim inviting her to submit to Monotheism. Bilqis sent gifts, which Sulaiman rejected, showing he cared for faith, not material tribute. Bilqis decided to visit him. Before she arrived, a Jinn with book knowledge (Asif ibn Barkhiya) brought her massive royal throne across hundreds of miles in the blink of an eye. When Bilqis entered Sulaiman's palace - which had a floor made of clear glass over flowing water - she pulled up her dress thinking it was deep water. Realizing the engineering marvel and Sulaiman's prophet status, she declared: "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulaiman to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (27:44).
• Death Leaning on his Staff: Sulaiman died while standing upright in prayer, leaning on his wooden staff. The Jinn continued performing hard labor for months, unaware that he was dead, until a wood-boring termite gnawed through his staff, causing his body to fall to the floor. This proved to humanity that Jinn have no knowledge of the unseen (Ghayb).

title: Prophet Ilyas (إلياس) / Elijah
narrative:
• Ilyas was sent to the northern Kingdom of Israel (Baalbek, in modern Lebanon). His people had abandoned the Torah and adopted the worship of a giant golden idol named Ba'al.
• Ilyas confronted their King and people: "Do you call upon Ba'al and leave the Best of Creators - Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?" (37:125-126).
• They called him a liar and plotted to kill him. Ilyas prayed for rain to be withheld, resulting in a three-year famine across the region. When the people realized their golden idol could not produce a drop of water, they sought Ilyas's help, though many remained stubborn in disbelief.

narrative:
• Al-Yasa' was the student, companion, and spiritual successor of Prophet Ilyas.
• After Ilyas passed away, Al-Yasa' continued calling the Israelites to uphold the Torah and Monotheism. The Quran honors him alongside Ismail, Dhul-Kifl, and Yunus as being specially favored above the worlds for their steadfast guidance.

title: Prophet Yunus (يونس) / Jonah (Dhun-Nun)
narrative:
• Leaving Nineveh: Yunus was sent to Nineveh (Mosul, Iraq), a population of over 100,000 people. Frustrated by their stubborn refusal to accept Monotheism, Yunus left the city in anger without waiting for explicit divine permission, warning them that punishment would strike in three days.
• In the Whale's Belly: Yunus boarded a crowded ship. Mid-journey, a severe storm threatened to sink the vessel. The crew drew lots to throw one passenger overboard to lighten the load. The lot fell on Yunus three times. Accepting God's decree, Yunus jumped into the sea. Allah commanded a giant whale to swallow Yunus whole without breaking his bones or flesh.
• The Darknesses & Dua: Trapped in three layers of darkness - the darkness of the night, the darkness of the deep ocean, and the darkness of the whale's belly - Yunus realized his error. He called out with the famous supplication: "La ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu minadh-dhalimin" ("There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers") (21:87).
• Restoration: Allah heard his prayer and commanded the whale to cast Yunus onto a barren shore. Exhausted and sick, Allah caused a gourd plant (Yaqtin) to grow over him, providing shade, protection from insects, and nourishment. Once healed, Yunus returned to Nineveh and discovered that after he left, the entire city realized their mistake, repented sincerely, and embraced faith - becoming the only whole nation in history saved from imminent punishment due to collective repentance (10:98).

title: Prophet Zakariya (زكريا) / Zechariah
narrative:
• Guardian of Maryam: Zakariya was a high priest of the Israelites and the guardian of young Maryam (Mary). title: Prophet 'Isa (عيسى) / Jesus, Son of Maryam
narrative:
• Miraculous Conception: Angel Jibreel appeared to the virgin Maryam in human form to announce the birth of a holy son created without a father, by Allah's command: "Be," and he is (3:47). Maryam withdrew to a remote place near a palm tree to give birth. Overcome by labor pains and distress, Allah provided her with a stream of fresh water at her feet and fresh dates from the shaken palm tree.
• Speaking from the Cradle: Maryam returned to her people carrying baby 'Isa. Her community accused her of immorality. Fulfilling Allah's instruction, Maryam remained silent and pointed to her infant. Miraculously, baby 'Isa spoke clearly from his cradle: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet. And He has made me blessed wherever I am..." (19:30-31), clearing his mother's honor instantly.
• Miracles of 'Isa: Allah granted 'Isa the Gospel (Injeel) and exceptional miracles: shaping birds out of clay and breathing life into them by Allah's leave, curing the blind and lepers, raising the dead to life, and describing what people had eaten or hidden in their homes.
• The Heavenly Table (Al-Ma'idah): His disciples (Al-Hawariyyun) requested a miracle to reassure their hearts: a table laid with food descending directly from heaven. 'Isa prayed, and Allah sent down the feast, warning that anyone who disbelieved after such a clear sign would face an unprecedented punishment.
• Saved from Crucifixion: When hostile groups plotted to kill 'Isa, Allah saved him. The Quran explicitly clarifies: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but another was made to resemble him to them... Rather, Allah raised him to Himself" (4:157-158). 'Isa was raised alive to heaven and will return near the end of time as a just leader to restore justice and establish Monotheism.

title: Prophet Muhammad (محمد) pbuh - The Final Messenger
display_title: Prophet Muhammad pbuh The Final Messenger
surah_citations: Al-Ahzab (33:40), Al-Fath (48:28-29), Muhammad (47:2), Al-Isra (17:1), Al-Anbiya (21:107), Surah An-Najm (53:1-18).
narrative:
• Early Life & Revelation: Born in Makkah in 570 CE in the Quraysh tribe, known before prophethood as Al-Amin (The Trustworthy). At age 40, while reflecting in the Cave of Hira, Angel Jibreel appeared to him with the first revelation: "Read in the name of your Lord who created..." (Surah Al-Alaq 96:1).
• Makkan Persecution & Night Journey: For 13 years in Makkah, he called people to abandon idol worship. Early Muslims faced torture, economic boycotts, and martyrdom. Following the loss of his wife Khadijah and uncle Abu Talib, Allah granted him the Isra and Mi'raj - traveling in one night from Makkah to Jerusalem, and ascending through the seven heavens to receive the command of five daily prayers.
• Madinah & Victory: He migrated (Hijrah) to Madinah, establishing the first Islamic society based on brotherhood between the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and Helpers (Ansar). After major defensive struggles (Badr, Uhud, Ahzab) and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, he led 10,000 Muslims in the peaceful Conquest of Makkah in 8 AH. He cleansed the Kaaba of 360 idols while granting general amnesty to his former persecutors: "Go, for you are free."
• Completion of Message: Delivering his Farewell Sermon at Mount Arafat, the final verse was revealed: "This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as your religion" (5:3). He passed away in 11 AH (632 CE) in Madinah.

title: Luqman the Wise (لقمان الحكيم)
narrative:
• Luqman was an Ethiopian/Nubian sage granted immense practical wisdom by Allah. The Quran records his tender advice to his son, which serves as a timeless parenting template:
 1. Monotheism: Never set up partners with Allah; shirk is the greatest injustice.
 2. Parental Duty: Honor parents, especially mothers who bear children through hardship upon hardship.
 3. Accountability: Every action, even the weight of a mustard seed hidden inside a rock or anywhere in the heavens or earth, will be brought forth by Allah.
 4. Daily Practices: Establish prayer, enjoin good, forbid evil, and bear trials patiently.
 5. Social Manners: Do not turn your cheek away from people in arrogance, do not walk boastfully on earth, moderate your step, and lower your voice - for the harshest of sounds is the braying of a donkey.

title: Dhul-Qarnayn (ذو القرنين) - The Righteous King
narrative:
• A powerful monotheist king given vast resources and military capabilities by Allah.
• He made three major expeditions:
 1. To the West: Reached the setting place of the sun (from his perspective on the coast), finding it setting near a murky body of water, where he established justice over local populations.
 2. To the East: Reached a land where people had no shelter from the intense sun, treating them with fairness.
 3. Between the Two Mountains: Met a tribe that barely understood human language. They pleaded for help against the barbaric tribes of Yajuj and Majuj (Gog and Magog) who raided their lands. Refusing monetary payment, Dhul-Qarnayn asked for manual labor and constructed a massive barrier using iron blocks poured over with molten copper. This wall traps Yajuj and Majuj until near the Day of Judgment.

• Musa requested to follow Khidr to learn wisdom. Khidr agreed on one condition: Musa must not question any of his actions until Khidr explained them himself.

 3. Rebuilding a Wall: Repaired a crumbling wall in a town that refused them basic hospitality. Reason: The wall belonged to two poor orphans, and buried beneath it was a treasure left by their late righteous father. Rebuilding it preserved the treasure until the orphans reached maturity.

display_title: Ashab al Kahf People of the Cave
narrative:
• A group of monotheistic young men lived under a pagan Roman emperor (Decius) who forced citizens to worship idols under pain of death.
• Refusing to abandon their faith, the youth fled into a mountain cave, accompanied by their faithful dog (Kitmir). They prayed for divine protection.
• Allah put them into a deep sleep lasting 309 lunar years (300 solar years). Allah caused them to turn over on their right and left sides so their bodies would not decay, while their dog lay stretching its forelegs at the cave entrance.
• When they woke up, thinking they had slept only a day or half a day, they sent one companion into town with a silver coin to buy clean food. The shopkeepers were amazed by the ancient currency, realizing that society had converted to Christianity/Monotheism centuries ago.

title: Talut (طالوت) / Saul

title: Habil and Qabil (هابيل وهابيل) / Abel and Cain
display_title: Habil and Qabil Abel and Cain
narrative:
• The two sons of Adam were instructed to offer a sacrifice to Allah to resolve a marriage dispute. Habil (a shepherd) brought his finest, healthy ram with complete sincerity. Qabil (a farmer) stingily brought his worst, ruined crops.
• Allah accepted Habil's sacrifice (consumed by a divine fire from the sky) and rejected Qabil's. Consumed by jealousy, Qabil threatened: "I will surely kill you!" Habil peacefully replied: "Allah only accepts from those who fear Him... If you raise your hand against me to kill me, I shall not raise my hand against you to kill you" (5:27-28).
• Qabil murdered Habil, committing the first homicide in human history. Unsure what to do with his brother's corpse, Allah sent a raven that scratched the earth to bury another dead bird. Seeing this, Qabil wept in remorse: "Woe to me! Have I failed to be like this raven and bury the body of my brother?" (5:31).

title: Ashab al-Sabt (The Sabbath Breakers)
narrative:
• The Test of the Fish: A community of Israelites lived in a seaside town (traditionally Aylah). They were commanded by Allah to observe the Sabbath (Saturday) strictly, meaning no working or fishing. To test their obedience, Allah caused the fish to appear abundantly on the surface of the water only on Saturdays, while completely disappearing on the other days of the week.
• The Trickery: Unable to resist the temptation, a group of townsfolk devised a trick. According to Tafsir Ibn Kathir, they dug trenches leading to pools on Friday. When the fish came in with the tide on Saturday, they were trapped in the pools. The people would then simply collect the trapped fish on Sunday, falsely claiming they hadn't "fished" on the Sabbath.
• The Three Groups and the Punishment: The town split into three groups: the sinners who broke the law, a righteous group who actively warned them to stop, and a third group who stayed silent and told the warners, "Why do you advise a people whom Allah is about to destroy?" (7:164). When the punishment came, Allah saved the warners, but cursed the sinners who used deceit to bypass God's laws, transforming them physically into despised monkeys and apes (2:65).

title: Ashab al-Ukhdud (The People of the Ditch)
narrative:
• The Boy and the King: Detailed heavily in Sahih Muslim, a tyrannical king in ancient Yemen forced his people to worship him. He assigned a young boy to learn from the royal magician. On his way to the magician, the boy met a pious monk who taught him pure Monotheism. The boy began performing miracles by Allah's permission, such as healing the blind and curing lepers.
• The Martyrdom: When the King found out, he tried to kill the boy by throwing him off a mountain and drowning him in the sea, but Allah saved the boy both times. The boy told the King, "You cannot kill me unless you gather the people, tie me to a trunk, and shoot an arrow saying: 'In the Name of Allah, the Lord of the boy.'" The King did this, and the boy died. Witnessing this ultimate sacrifice, the entire crowd shouted, "We believe in the Lord of the boy!"
• The Trenches of Fire: Furious, the King ordered massive trenches (Ukhdud) to be dug in the streets, filled with roaring fires. He commanded that any citizen who refused to abandon their belief in Allah be thrown in alive.
• The Speaking Baby: During the slaughter, a believing woman hesitated at the edge of the fire because she was holding her nursing baby. Miraculously, Allah allowed the infant to speak, telling her: "O mother! Be patient, for you are upon the Truth." Encouraged, she stepped into the flames.

title: Ashab al-Fil (The People of the Elephant)
narrative:
• The Jealousy of Abraha: In the year Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was born (570 CE, known as the Year of the Elephant), a Christian Abyssinian ruler of Yemen named Abraha built a magnificent, towering cathedral called Al-Qullays. He intended to divert the Arab pilgrimage away from the Kaaba in Makkah to his new church. Infuriated, a man from an Arab tribe traveled to Yemen and defiled the cathedral at night.
• The March on Makkah: Enraged, Abraha marched on Makkah with a massive army, bringing along a gigantic war elephant named Mahmud. The Makkan tribes, knowing they could not defeat the army, evacuated to the surrounding mountains. Abdul Muttalib (the Prophet's grandfather) told Abraha, "I am the lord of my camels, but the House (the Kaaba) has a Lord who will protect it."
• The Divine Defense: As Abraha's army lined up to destroy the Kaaba, the elephant Mahmud knelt on the ground and stubbornly refused to move toward Makkah, though he would willingly run in any other direction. Suddenly, Allah sent flocks of birds (Ababil) sweeping in from the sea. Each bird carried three small, baked clay stones (Sijjil) - one in its beak and two in its claws. The birds dropped the stones like rain. The stones pierced straight through the soldiers and their armor, leaving them completely destroyed, like "eaten straw" (105:5).

title: The People of Saba (Sheba)
narrative:
• The Gardens of Prosperity: The people of Saba lived in modern-day Yemen. They were blessed with a massive engineering marvel known as the Ma'rib Dam. This dam captured rainwater and channeled it to irrigate two vast, spectacular gardens that flanked their city on the right and left. The land was so fruitful and secure that they could travel for days from village to village without ever needing to pack provisions or fear for their safety.
• Ingratitude and Arrogance: Instead of being thankful, the people became arrogant. They actually complained about their ease and safety, foolishly asking Allah to make their journeys longer and harder, distancing their stops. They also rejected the prophets sent to them.
• The Flood of 'Arim: As punishment for their profound ingratitude, Allah caused the destruction of their mighty dam. Classical Tafsir mentions that Allah sent a simple rat to gnaw at the foundation stones of the great dam until it weakened. The dam burst, unleashing a devastating flood (Sayl al-Arim) that entirely washed away their lush, luxurious paradise. In its place, Allah gave them two gardens producing only bitter, thorny fruit and sparse bushes. The once-great civilization of Saba was completely shattered, and its people were scattered across the earth.

title: Ashab al-Jannah (The Owners of the Garden)
narrative:
• The Righteous Father and Greedy Sons: A wealthy, righteous man owned a highly productive agricultural garden (orchard). When he harvested his crops, he made it a strict habit to give a generous portion of the produce to the poor and needy. When he passed away, his sons inherited the garden. Driven by greed, they whispered among themselves, deciding they would not give a single fruit to the poor.
• The Nighttime Plot: To avoid the beggars who would wait for the harvest, the brothers swore an oath to sneak out early in the morning and harvest everything in secret.
• The Black Ash: While they were sleeping, a devastating calamity (a fire) from Allah swept through their prized orchard at night. When the brothers arrived eagerly in the morning, they found their lush garden completely burned, turned black as pitch and ashes. At first, they thought they had taken a wrong turn and were lost. Then they realized the truth: "Rather, we have been deprived" (68:27).
• Repentance: The most moderate and wise among them reminded the others that he had told them to praise Allah. Realizing their grave sin of greed and plotting against the poor, they admitted their wrongdoing and sincerely repented, hoping Allah would replace their ruined garden with something better.
